title: The cowherd in autumn
hookLine: a cowherd guards the ripe crops with a stick, then rests under a tree once the harvest is in (MN 19)
last: TWO PILES — A PATH WORN ACROSS A FIELD.

cards: Late in the rains, the crops stand tall and green right up to the edge of the village paths. It's beautiful, and for a cowherd it's a nightmare. His cows want nothing more than to wander into those fields and eat.

If they do, he could be beaten, locked up, fined or blamed. So all day long he walks beside them with a stick, tapping and turning them back. Then the harvest comes in, the fields are bare, and everything changes.
In the sutta of two kinds of thought, the Buddha says his mind was like those cows.

teach.h: AUTUMN: A STICK AND THE RIPE CROPS.
teach.b: Here's the first season, from the Middle-Length Discourses, number nineteen.

In the last month of the rains, in autumn, when the crops are ripening, a cowherd guards his cows by tapping and poking them this way and that with a stick, because he sees the trouble that will come if they stray into the crops.
In the same way, the Buddha says, he saw the danger in unwholesome thoughts, and the blessing in letting them go.
That's the guarding: yesterday's two piles, done with attention, the stick tapping when the mind wanders toward ill will or craving. Then something surprising.

Even wholesome thinking, he says, if he kept it up too long, would tire his body, and a tired body strains the mind. So he steadied his mind inside, quieted it, and brought it together. Now the second season.

teach.h: HOT SEASON: REST UNDER A TREE.
teach.b: In the last month of the hot season, when all the crops have been brought into the village, the cowherd guards his cows while sitting at the foot of a tree or out in the open.
He only needs to be aware: there are the cows. No stick. No running.
That, the Buddha says, was all he needed then: simple awareness that those states were there. Two lessons sit in this one picture. Guarding the mind takes effort at the start, and that's fine.
But effort isn't the whole path.
There comes a time to put the stick down and rest under the tree, still aware, but at ease.

how: Meditation teachers often describe a balance of effort and ease, sometimes using the cowherd of MN 19: careful guarding of the mind at first, then relaxed awareness once the mind has settled.

o: a farmer who plows and sows the fields
a hunter who tracks wild animals
a cowherd, who guards the herd and then rests

games.q: match each season to what the cowherd does.
p: guards the cows with a stick
rests at the foot of a tree
tires the body and strains the mind

s: the Buddha says even wholesome thinking, kept up too long, can tire the body
so he steadied and quieted his mind.
in the hot season the cowherd still has to run after the cows with a stick
with the harvest in, he sits under a tree and just stays aware: there are the cows.
the cowherd guards the cows because he fears punishment if they eat the crops
the sutta lists beating, imprisonment, a fine and blame.

games.q: you're the cowherd. the harvest is in and the fields are bare. what do you do with the cows?
o: keep tapping them with the stick all day.
sit under a tree, just aware that the cows are there.
games.why: with no crops to protect, he rests at the foot of a tree, mindful that the cows are there; the Buddha says his mind needed only that awareness.

practice: For the first half of the sit, be the cowherd in autumn: watch the breath closely, and each time the mind wanders, tap it gently back.
Then let the stick go, as if sitting at the foot of a tree with the fields bare, and simply know: there's the breath, there are the thoughts. Nothing to herd; just aware, and at ease.

wordCard.voice: Gopalaka, a cowherd. Guarding the mind with care while the crops are ripe, then resting under a tree, simply aware, once the harvest is in.

orig.note: Pali gopālaka: a cowherd, from go, cow, and pāla, keeper.

carryVoice: Your line: guard, then rest. Effort has its season, and so does ease. Day three hundred sixty-one, done.

sources.ref: MN 19 (Dvedhavitakka Sutta), the two cowherd similes
